title: How I Reduced Voice AI Latency from 1.8 Seconds to Under 300ms in Production

body:
This article explains exactly how I reduced that latency to under 300ms, what was actually causing the delay, and the architectural changes that made the difference.

Introduction

A few months ago, I deployed a voice AI system for handling real-time phone calls.

On paper, everything looked correct. Speech-to-text was fast. The language model was responsive. Text-to-speech worked reliably.

But when we tested it with real users, the experience was unacceptable.

There was a consistent delay of around 1.5 to 2 seconds before the AI responded. People would pause, repeat themselves, or assume the system had failed. It didn’t feel like a conversation. It felt like waiting for a slow API.

That was the moment I realized something important:

Latency is not a metric in voice AI. It is the product itself.

This article explains exactly how I reduced that latency to under 300ms, what was actually causing the delay, and the architectural changes that made the difference.

The Initial Architecture (and Why It Failed)

The first version followed a straightforward pipeline:

User speaks → audio sent to backend → speech-to-text → full transcript → LLM → full response → text-to-speech → audio returned

This is the same pattern most backend engineers start with. It works fine for chat applications, but it breaks down completely in voice systems.

The key issue was that every step was blocking the next one.

We were waiting for:

  • the user to finish speaking
  • the full transcription to complete
  • the LLM to generate the entire response
  • the TTS engine to synthesize full audio

Only then did the system respond.

Even if each component was “fast,” the combined delay was too high.

Where the Latency Was Actually Coming From

After profiling the system, the breakdown looked like this:

  • Speech-to-text: ~400ms
  • LLM response: ~700ms
  • Text-to-speech: ~500ms
  • Network overhead: ~200ms

Total: ~1.8 seconds

What surprised me was that no single component was the problem. The issue was the sequential execution model.

The Shift That Changed Everything

The real fix was not optimizing individual services.

It was changing the flow from sequential processing to streaming.

Instead of waiting for complete data at each stage, I restructured the system to process partial data continuously.

This required rethinking the entire pipeline.

Step 1: Stop Waiting for the User to Finish Speaking

The first major improvement came from switching to streaming speech-to-text.

Instead of waiting for a full sentence, the system started receiving partial transcripts in real time.

For example, instead of:

“Hello, I need help with my billing issue”

we started getting:

“Hello”
“Hello, I need”
“Hello, I need help with…”

As soon as partial text arrived, it was forwarded downstream.

This alone removed several hundred milliseconds of idle waiting.

Step 2: Start the LLM Before the Sentence Ends

Initially, the LLM only ran after receiving the full transcript.

That was a mistake.

I modified the system so the LLM begins processing partial input as it arrives. The model starts forming a response before the user finishes speaking.

In practice, this means the AI is already “thinking” while the user is still talking.

This change reduced perceived latency significantly, even though the raw processing time of the model did not change.

Step 3: Stream the Response Instead of Waiting for It

Originally, the LLM response was generated as a complete block of text.

That introduced unnecessary delay.

Switching to streaming output allowed us to process the response token by token.

As soon as the first tokens were available, they were sent to the next stage instead of waiting for the full response.

This made the system feel much faster, because users heard the response begin almost immediately.

Step 4: Replace Traditional TTS with Streaming Audio

Text-to-speech was one of the biggest hidden bottlenecks.

Most TTS systems require the full input before generating audio. That means even if your LLM is fast, you still wait before playback begins.

The solution was to use a streaming TTS approach that converts partial text into audio chunks in real time.

Now, as soon as the first few words of the response are generated, audio playback begins.

This removed another large delay from the pipeline.

Step 5: Run Everything in Parallel

Even after introducing streaming, the system still had inefficiencies because components were loosely chained.

The final step was restructuring the backend to run all stages concurrently.

Speech recognition, language processing, and audio synthesis all operate as independent asynchronous streams.

Instead of this:

Step A → Step B → Step C

The system behaves like this:

  • STT is continuously producing text
  • LLM is continuously consuming and producing tokens
  • TTS is continuously generating audio

All three run at the same time.

This is the core principle behind low-latency systems used in real-time communication platforms.

Step 6: Move Processing Closer to the Media Layer

Another issue was network delay.

Initially, audio was sent to a central backend for processing. This added unnecessary round-trip time.

The improvement came from moving processing closer to where the audio stream was handled.

In practical terms, this means:

  • keeping media handling and AI processing in the same region
  • reducing hops between services
  • avoiding unnecessary API gateways in the critical path

This is a pattern commonly used in real-time systems where every millisecond matters.

Step 7: Maintain Stateful Sessions

One subtle but important optimization was removing repeated context loading.

Originally, each request required rebuilding conversation context from storage.

Instead, I kept session state in memory for the duration of the call.

This avoided repeated database calls and reduced processing time for every interaction.

Final Results

After applying these changes, the latency breakdown improved to:

  • Streaming STT: ~100ms
  • LLM (streaming): ~150ms
  • Streaming TTS: ~100ms
  • Network: ~50ms

Total: around 250 to 300ms

More importantly, the system felt responsive. Users stopped interrupting or repeating themselves. Conversations became natural.

What Actually Matters in Voice AI

The biggest lesson from this experience is that optimizing individual components is not enough.

You can have the fastest speech model, the best LLM, and a high-quality TTS engine, and still end up with a slow system.

What matters is how data flows between them.

Low latency comes from:

  • streaming instead of batching
  • parallel execution instead of sequential pipelines
  • early processing instead of waiting for completion
  • minimizing network distance

Closing Thoughts

Most backend systems are designed around request-response cycles.

Voice AI systems are not.

They behave more like real-time systems, where data is constantly flowing and every delay is noticeable.

Once you shift your thinking from APIs to streams, the problem becomes much clearer and much easier to solve.
